<RichText>
# SQLite WAL mode failure modes for single-writer multi-reader desktop apps

**Run stats:** 2 participants, 2 extraction reports, 2 cross-reviews, 1 curator; started 2026-08-29T18:23:39Z. **Participants:** hermes · openai · gpt-5.6-luna · effort low; hermes · google · gemini-3.7-flash · effort low. **Curator:** hermes · openai · gpt-5.6-luna · effort low.
</RichText>

<Callout tone="warning">
This is multi-model synthesis, not verified truth. Verify consequential claims before acting.
</Callout>

<Section title="Question">
<RichText>
What are the real failure modes of relying on SQLite WAL mode for a single-writer multi-reader desktop app, and when do you need something else?
</RichText>
</Section>

<Section title="Final answer">
<RichText>
WAL mode is the right default for a single-writer, multi-reader desktop app on a local filesystem. Both extractions independently confirm this (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash). The read/write concurrency model works as advertised — one writer appends to the WAL file, many readers read concurrently without blocking. The failure modes are about the assumptions WAL silently embeds and the edge cases where those assumptions break.

**1. Filesystem incompatibility.** WAL requires shared memory (the `-shm` file, via mmap) and POSIX byte-range locks. Network filesystems (NFS, SMB/CIFS, some FUSE) cannot share memory across hosts, so WAL silently falls back to `delete` mode or corrupts the database (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash). macOS App Sandbox can block creation of the journal files SQLite needs (openai · gpt-5.6-luna). Cloud-synced folders (iCloud Drive, Dropbox, Google Drive) may copy the `.db` file without the matching `-wal` and `-shm` files, leaving the remote copy inconsistent or corrupt (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

**2. Checkpoint starvation.** A long-running read transaction prevents the WAL from being checkpointed, so the `-wal` file grows without bound, degrading read performance and consuming disk space (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash). A single persistent read connection — common for UI refresh loops — can starve checkpoints even if no individual transaction is long-lived (openai · gpt-5.6-luna). The WAL file does not shrink after a checkpoint by default; it retains its high-water size unless `PRAGMA journal_size_limit` is set or `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` is run (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

**3. Surprising SQLITE_BUSY on readers.** Readers can get `SQLITE_BUSY` with no application write in progress: during connection open/close (the `-shm` file briefly requires an exclusive lock), during crash recovery, and when another connection holds the database in exclusive locking mode (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash). Bursty short-lived read-only connections with no busy timeout are the worst case — a reproducer by Hynek Schlawack shows 7 of 6400 such connections fail with `database is locked` (google · gemini-3.7-flash). Setting a `busy_timeout` eliminates this (google · gemini-3.7-flash).

**4. Data loss on unclean shutdown.** If the app crashes without closing its connection or checkpointing, committed transactions that exist only in the WAL file can be lost (openai · gpt-5.6-luna). With `synchronous=NORMAL` (the recommended WAL pairing), transactions committed since the last checkpoint are not fsync'd to disk and can be lost on power failure — the database does not corrupt, but data is lost (openai · gpt-5.6-luna). A read-only connection as the last to close leaves `-wal` and `-shm` files on disk without running the final cleanup checkpoint (google · gemini-3.7-flash; openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

**5. The WAL-reset corruption bug.** A data race between concurrent checkpoint and write operations can cause a checkpoint to skip a committed transaction, corrupting the database file (openai · gpt-5.6-luna). The bug existed from SQLite 3.7.0 through 3.51.2, fixed in 3.51.3 (2026-03-13), with backports for 3.44.6 and 3.50.7 (openai · gpt-5.6-luna). SQLite's telemetry says the occurrence rate is comparable to SSD malfunctions or cosmic-ray hits, but Tailscale reported 19 separate corruption incidents over 6 months in their production control plane with aggressive 250ms checkpointing (google · gemini-3.7-flash). Two independent reproducers confirmed the bug is reachable with generic concurrent write/checkpoint workloads: Carl Sverre triggered it in 15 minutes on Antithesis, and Phil Eaton reproduced it with a roughly 100-line C program using the public SQLite API (google · gemini-3.7-flash). The original extraction by openai · gpt-5.6-luna conflated these two reproducers — Carl Sverre authored the Antithesis run and the 15-minute figure; Phil Eaton authored the separate theconsensus.dev reproducer (google · gemini-3.7-flash).

**When you need something else:**

- Your database lives on a network filesystem or cloud-synced folder — use a client-server database or replicate with Litestream or LiteFS.
- You need true multi-writer concurrency — SQLite is fundamentally single-writer; step up to PostgreSQL or similar.
- You distribute a database on read-only media — convert to `journal_mode=DELETE` before burning. Opening a WAL database read-only requires either pre-existing `-shm` and `-wal` files or write access to the containing directory (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).
- Your SQLite version is below 3.51.3 and you run concurrent WAL connections — the WAL-reset bug is a corruption risk worth patching.
- You cannot tolerate any reader seeing `SQLITE_BUSY` and cannot set a busy timeout.
- Very large transactions (over 100MB) on SQLite versions below 3.11.0 — on modern SQLite, the large-transaction performance disadvantage is withdrawn per the documentation (google · gemini-3.7-flash; openai · gpt-5.6-luna). The cross-reviews from both participants confirmed the original guidance is struck through and superseded.

<Section title="Knowledge map">
<Tabs>
<Tab label="Shared core">
<RichText>
Claims both extractions made independently — repetition, not proof:

- WAL is the right default for a single-writer, multi-reader desktop app on a local filesystem (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- Checkpoint starvation: a long-running read transaction prevents WAL checkpointing, causing unbounded WAL growth (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- WAL does not work over network filesystems — it requires shared memory that cannot span hosts (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- SQLITE_BUSY can still occur in WAL mode during connection open/close, crash recovery, and exclusive locking (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- Page size cannot be changed while in WAL mode — you must exit to rollback journal mode first (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- A read-only connection as the last to close leaves `-wal` and `-shm` files on disk without running the final cleanup checkpoint (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- EXCLUSIVE locking mode eliminates the `-shm` file but locks the database to a single process (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
</RichText>
</Tab>
<Tab label="Unique finds">
<RichText>
Kept even with a support count of one — consensus is repetition, not truth:

- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** The WAL-reset bug (wal.html section 11) is a corruption-class failure mode for multi-connection WAL databases, fixed in 3.51.3 with backports for 3.44.6 and 3.50.7.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** Unclean shutdown can lose committed transactions that exist only in the WAL file — a checkpoint before exit or closing the connection preserves all data.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** `synchronous=NORMAL` in WAL mode sacrifices post-checkpoint transaction durability on power loss — no corruption, but data is lost.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** A single bit flip in the WAL file can silently lose committed entries (BreakingSQLite project) — SQLite does not add redundancy for error detection.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** The WAL file does not shrink after a checkpoint by default; set `PRAGMA journal_size_limit` or run `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` to reclaim space.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` is persistent — stored in the database file header, surviving close and reopen.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** Cross-database transactions spanning ATTACHed databases are atomic per-database but not as a set.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** WAL mode slightly degrades read-heavy, write-rare workloads by about 1 to 2 percent.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** Bursty short-lived read-only connections can get SQLITE_BUSY with no writes in progress — Hynek Schlawack's reproducer shows 7 of 6400 failures; a busy timeout eliminates this.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** Read-only connections in WAL mode still write to the `-shm` file — "read-only" is a misnomer on the filesystem side.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** The checkpoint must stop at the oldest reader's end mark, so even a single long-running analytical query can pin the entire WAL.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** POSIX file locks are process-scoped, not connection-scoped — a single process with multiple connections shares one lock set.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** The `-shm` file is never fsync'd to disk; it is rebuilt from the WAL on recovery.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** Tailscale reported 19 separate WAL-reset corruption incidents over 6 months in production with 250ms checkpointing — the primary source for real-world frequency.
</RichText>
</Tab>
<Tab label="Contradictions">
<RichText>
**1. WAL-reset bug frequency: official telemetry vs. reproducer evidence (unresolved).**

openai · gpt-5.6-luna cites SQLite telemetry saying the occurrence rate is comparable to SSD malfunctions or cosmic-ray hits. google · gemini-3.7-flash cites Tailscale's 19 production incidents over 6 months and two independent reproducers (Carl Sverre on Antithesis in 15 minutes; Phil Eaton locally in seconds). The truth is likely that the bug is reachable with sustained concurrent write/checkpoint activity over long runtimes, but rare enough that most short-lived desktop sessions never hit it. Both positions appear; verify before relying on either.

**2. Large-transaction guidance: withdrawn or still active (resolved by cross-review).**

openai · gpt-5.6-luna said the guidance "partially improved but remains." google · gemini-3.7-flash said the docs "still recommend" rollback modes for large transactions. Both cross-reviews challenge these characterizations: the SQLite documentation strikes through the original text and replaces it with "Beginning with version 3.11.0, WAL mode works as efficiently with large transactions as does rollback mode." The guidance is withdrawn for modern SQLite. The space concern (large transactions cause large WAL files) remains valid but is separate from the performance recommendation.

**3. Reproducer attribution (resolved by cross-review).**

openai · gpt-5.6-luna attributed the Antithesis 15-minute reproducer to Phil Eaton. google · gemini-3.7-flash identified two separate reproducers: Carl Sverre authored the Antithesis run; Phil Eaton authored the independent theconsensus.dev reproducer using the public API. The cross-review from google · gemini-3.7-flash is correct — these are two distinct people using two different methods.
</RichText>
</Tab>
